question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355, a business entity seeking to act as a real estate broker must designate one of its managing officers as its broker for purposes of the Real Estate License Act. This designation requirement means:
choice_a: The entity itself is not the license holder in a functional sense -- a specific individual managing officer must hold the entity's broker designation and be personally accountable
choice_b: Any employee of the entity, licensed or not, may be named as the designated broker
choice_c: The requirement is satisfied automatically once the entity registers with the Texas Secretary of State
choice_d: A designated broker is only needed if the entity has more than ten employees
explanation: Section 1101.355(a)(1) requires a business entity to designate one of its managing officers as its broker, tying the entity's brokerage license to a specific accountable individual rather than to the entity's corporate existence alone.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(a)(1) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: A business entity applying for a TREC broker license has a designated broker who owns only 4 percent of the entity. Under Section 1101.355, this ownership structure triggers which additional requirement?
choice_a: The entity must supply documentation showing it maintains errors and omissions insurance with a minimum $1 million annual occurrence limit
choice_b: The designated broker must immediately increase their ownership stake to at least 10 percent
choice_c: The entity is barred from holding a broker license unless the designated broker owns a majority interest
choice_d: No additional requirement applies; ownership percentage is irrelevant to any licensing condition
explanation: Section 1101.355(a)(2) requires a business entity to document errors and omissions insurance with a minimum $1 million annual occurrence limit specifically when the designated broker owns less than 10 percent of the entity, addressing the reduced personal financial stake such a designated broker has in the entity's liability exposure.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(a)(2) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: A business entity's designated broker must, at all times, satisfy which status requirement under Section 1101.355(b)?
choice_a: Be a licensed individual broker in active status and good standing according to the Commission's records
choice_b: Hold only a sales agent license, since the entity itself supplies the broker license
choice_c: Be a shareholder owning at least 50 percent of the entity
choice_d: Have no disciplinary history requirement, since only the entity's record matters
explanation: Section 1101.355(b) provides that a business entity may not act as a broker unless its designated broker is a licensed individual broker in active status and good standing according to the Commission's records -- the entity's authority to act as a broker is entirely derivative of that individual's standing.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(b) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: In determining whether a business entity's designated broker is in "good standing" for purposes of Section 1101.355, TREC may consider which factors?
choice_a: The disciplinary background of the broker or of any entity for which the broker currently or previously served as designated broker, and whether amounts owed to the Commission by the broker or those entities have been paid
choice_b: Only the broker's personal credit score
choice_c: Only whether the broker has ever changed employers
choice_d: Only the number of years the broker has held an active license, with no regard to disciplinary or payment history
explanation: Section 1101.355(b-1) allows the Commission to weigh both the disciplinary history connected to the broker (personally or through entities the broker has been designated broker for) and the payment status of any amounts owed to the Commission when evaluating good standing.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(b-1) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: As a baseline rule under Section 1101.355(c), a business entity that receives compensation on behalf of a license holder for real estate brokerage activity must:
choice_a: Itself be licensed as a broker under Chapter 1101
choice_b: Register with the county clerk only, with no involvement from TREC
choice_c: Obtain a federal employer identification number, which alone satisfies all state licensing obligations
choice_d: Do nothing further, since compensation flowing to an entity is entirely outside TREC's jurisdiction
explanation: Section 1101.355(c) establishes that a business entity receiving compensation on behalf of a license holder for brokerage activity must itself hold a broker license -- this is the general rule that a narrow statutory exception (for certain wholly licensee-owned entities) departs from.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(c) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: A sales agent forms a single-member LLC solely to receive their own commission checks from their sponsoring broker for tax and liability-structuring purposes; the LLC performs no other brokerage functions. Under Section 1101.355(d), this LLC can avoid the full broker-licensing requirement if it:
choice_a: Is an LLC or S corporation at least 51 percent owned by the license holder receiving the compensation, performs no other broker functions, and is registered with the Commission
choice_b: Is instead converted into a general partnership with no ownership restrictions
choice_c: Simply avoids ever depositing the commission checks into a business bank account
choice_d: Hires its own separately licensed broker distinct from the sales agent who formed it
explanation: Section 1101.355(d) creates a narrow exception: an LLC or S corporation that is at least 51 percent owned by the license holder receiving the compensation, performs no broker functions beyond receiving that compensation, and maintains Commission registration can receive licensed compensation without itself becoming a fully licensed broker entity.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(d)-(e) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: Separate from the business-entity compensation rule, TREC guidance recognizes that an entirely unlicensed person may lawfully share in income earned by a real estate brokerage under which condition?
choice_a: Only if the unlicensed person engages in no acts for which a real estate license is required
choice_b: Never, under any circumstances, regardless of what activities the person performs
choice_c: Only if the unlicensed person is a family member of the broker
choice_d: Only if the amount shared is under $500
explanation: An unlicensed person -- such as an office bookkeeper receiving a bonus tied to office revenue, or a referral source paid under a lawful non-brokerage arrangement -- may share in brokerage income so long as that person performs no acts requiring a real estate license; the moment licensed activity is involved, licensing (or the narrow entity exception) is required.
source_note: TREC Frequently Asked Questions (Compensation); Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.351 (License Required)

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552, a resident Texas broker's obligation regarding a physical office is:
choice_a: The broker must maintain a fixed office in the state, and the office address must be designated on the broker's license
choice_b: No physical office is ever required for a resident broker
choice_c: A fixed office is required only if the broker sponsors more than one sales agent
choice_d: The office address is optional information that need not appear on the license record
explanation: Section 1101.552(a) requires a resident broker to maintain a fixed office in Texas, with that office's address designated on the broker's license record -- the statutory foundation underlying TREC's place-of-business registration requirements.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552(a) (Fixed Office Required; Change of Address)

question: A Texas resident broker relocates their office to a new address. Under Section 1101.552(b), within how many days must the broker apply for a new license reflecting the updated office location?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 90 days
choice_c: One year
choice_d: There is no deadline; the broker may update the address at the next renewal
explanation: Section 1101.552(b) requires a broker who relocates to apply for a new license reflecting the updated office address within 10 days of the move, and the Commission issues a revised license once the new address satisfies statutory requirements.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552(b) (Fixed Office Required; Change of Address)

question: A broker licensed in Texas but who resides in and primarily operates from another state is classified as a nonresident broker. Under Section 1101.552(d), such a broker:
choice_a: Is not required to maintain a place of business in Texas
choice_b: Must maintain an in-state office identical to a resident broker's obligation
choice_c: Must maintain two separate offices, one in Texas and one in the home state
choice_d: Is prohibited from holding a Texas broker license under any circumstances
explanation: Section 1101.552(d) exempts a nonresident licensed broker from the fixed-office requirement imposed on resident brokers, recognizing that a nonresident broker's business operations are centered outside Texas.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552(d) (Fixed Office Required; Change of Address)

question: Beyond maintaining a fixed office, Section 1101.552(e) requires a license holder to:
choice_a: Provide the Commission with current contact information, including mailing address, phone number, and business email if available, and notify the Commission of any changes
choice_b: Publish their home address publicly on their brokerage website
choice_c: File a new fixed-office application every calendar year regardless of whether anything changed
choice_d: Report contact information only to the local county clerk, not to TREC
explanation: Section 1101.552(e) obligates every license holder to keep the Commission apprised of current contact details -- mailing address, phone, and business email where available -- and to notify TREC promptly of any change, ensuring the Commission can reliably reach license holders.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552(e) (Fixed Office Required; Change of Address)

question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.155, every real estate advertisement must include, in a readily noticeable location, which item at minimum?
choice_a: The name of the license holder or team placing the advertisement
choice_b: The square footage of the brokerage's main office
choice_c: A copy of the broker's E&O insurance policy number
choice_d: The advertising license holder's personal cell phone carrier
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.155 requires that every advertisement include, in a readily noticeable location, the name of the license holder or team placing the advertisement, so a consumer can identify who is responsible for the marketing.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements)

question: A sponsored sales agent advertises a listing using a registered team name in large, prominent lettering. Under 22 TAC Section 535.155's size requirement, the sponsoring broker's name in that advertisement must appear:
choice_a: In at least half the size of the largest contact information for any sales agent, associated broker, or team name contained in the advertisement
choice_b: In exactly the same font as the team name, with no size ratio requirement
choice_c: Only on a separate webpage linked from the advertisement, never within the ad itself
choice_d: In print no larger than a standard business card, regardless of the ad's overall size
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.155 sets a specific size ratio: the broker's name must appear in at least half the size of the largest contact information for any sales agent, associated broker, or team name shown in the advertisement, preventing the broker's identity from being visually buried.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements)

question: A team's advertisement uses a stylized logo that incorporates the broker's name as graphic art alongside decorative icons and a tagline. For purposes of the Section 535.155 size-ratio rule, which portion of that logo is measured against the largest contact information in the ad?
choice_a: Only the size of the broker's name text itself within the logo, not the logo's decorative elements as a whole
choice_b: The entire logo graphic, including all icons and taglines, measured as a single unit
choice_c: Nothing; logos are entirely exempt from the size-ratio requirement
choice_d: Only the tagline text, since the broker's name is presumed compliant whenever it appears anywhere in a logo
explanation: TREC guidance on Section 535.155 clarifies that when a broker's name appears within a logo, it is the size of the broker's name text itself -- not the logo's full graphic footprint -- that must be measured against the required at-least-half-size ratio.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements); TREC Frequently Asked Questions (Advertising)

question: A brokerage's yard sign displays only the broker's own company name and logo, with no individual agent or team name referenced anywhere on the sign. Under TREC's advertising rules, this sign is:
choice_a: Permissible, since a broker's name may appear alone on advertising materials without triggering the size-ratio comparison that applies once an agent's or team's name is added
choice_b: A violation, because every sign must list every sponsored agent by name
choice_c: A violation, because a sign must always include a team name even if no team is involved
choice_d: Only permissible if the sign also lists the broker's home address
explanation: TREC guidance confirms a broker's name alone is acceptable on advertising materials; the size-ratio requirement under Section 535.155 is triggered specifically by the inclusion of a sales agent, associated broker, or team name that could otherwise overshadow the broker's identity.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements); TREC Frequently Asked Questions (Advertising)

question: A sales agent posts "JUST SOLD!" marketing for a property on social media despite having had no involvement -- as either the listing agent or a buyer's agent -- in that transaction. Under TREC advertising standards, this practice is:
choice_a: Misleading advertising, because a licensee may only claim credit for having "sold" a property if they actually worked with the seller or the buyer in the transaction that resulted in the sale
choice_b: Permitted, since any licensee may advertise any closed sale in the local market regardless of involvement
choice_c: Permitted only if the agent obtains after-the-fact permission from the listing brokerage
choice_d: A matter entirely outside TREC's advertising jurisdiction because it involves a closed, not active, listing
explanation: TREC guidance treats "just sold" or similar sold-credit advertising as misleading unless the advertising licensee actually worked with the seller or the buyer in the transaction that resulted in the sale -- borrowing credit for a closing the licensee had no role in misrepresents the licensee's track record to consumers.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements); TREC Frequently Asked Questions (Advertising)

question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.154, a registered team name used by a group of sponsored sales agents within a brokerage must, at minimum, satisfy which naming convention?
choice_a: End with the word "team" or "group"
choice_b: Include the individual last name of every team member
choice_c: Be identical to the brokerage's own registered assumed business name
choice_d: Contain a number indicating how many agents belong to the team
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.154 requires a team name to end with "team" or "group," a naming convention designed to signal to consumers that they are dealing with a group operating under a licensed broker rather than a standalone brokerage.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.154, a proposed team name that includes the word "Brokerage" or "Company" within it would most likely be rejected because:
choice_a: Team names may not contain words that falsely imply the team itself is an independent brokerage entity, since a team operates under -- not as -- a licensed broker
choice_b: TREC prohibits the use of any English-language business terms in team names
choice_c: Such words are reserved exclusively for federally chartered corporations
choice_d: There is no such restriction; any wording is permitted in a team name
explanation: Because a team is a marketing designation for sponsored agents operating under a licensed broker -- not a separately licensed brokerage -- 22 TAC Section 535.154 bars team names from including words like "brokerage" or "company" that would misleadingly suggest independent brokerage status.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: When a group of sponsored sales agents wants to begin marketing under a team name, whose responsibility is it to register that team name under 22 TAC Section 535.154?
choice_a: The sponsoring broker registers the team name, not the individual sales agents who make up the team
choice_b: Each individual sales agent must separately register the identical team name under their own license
choice_c: No registration of any kind is required for a team name
choice_d: The Texas Secretary of State registers all real estate team names directly, bypassing TREC and the broker entirely
explanation: The sponsoring broker -- who bears ultimate responsibility for advertising compliance under the broker responsibility rule -- registers the team name under 22 TAC Section 535.154, not the individual sales agents using it, keeping accountability anchored to the broker.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: A broker wants to market the brokerage under a catchy assumed business name (DBA) rather than the broker's name as licensed. Under 22 TAC Section 535.154, before that DBA can be used in advertising, the broker must provide proof of legal authority to use the name, which is typically established by:
choice_a: An assumed name filing with the Texas Secretary of State or a county clerk's assumed name certificate
choice_b: A verbal confirmation from any TREC staff member
choice_c: A trademark registered with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, which is the only acceptable proof
choice_d: Nothing; assumed business names require no proof of legal authority to use
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.154 requires a broker registering an assumed business name to demonstrate legal authority to use it, which is generally shown through an assumed name filing with the Secretary of State or a county clerk's assumed name (DBA) certificate.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: A brokerage has properly registered an assumed business name (DBA) with TREC. Compared to a registered team name, this DBA differs in one important respect:
choice_a: The DBA may be used in advertising by any of the broker's sponsored agents, while a team name is limited to use by the members of that specific team
choice_b: The DBA can only be used by the broker personally and never by any sponsored agent
choice_c: A DBA requires no legal-authority documentation, while a team name always requires a Secretary of State filing
choice_d: There is no functional difference; DBAs and team names are interchangeable under TREC rules
explanation: A properly registered assumed business name belongs to the broker's overall business and may be used broadly across the brokerage's sponsored agents, while a registered team name is tied specifically to the agents who make up that team -- a meaningful scope distinction under 22 TAC Section 535.154.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: A sales agent, without informing the sponsoring broker, begins advertising under a catchy business name the agent invented independently, never submitted for registration. Under 22 TAC Section 535.154, this conduct is problematic primarily because:
choice_a: A license holder may not advertise under an alternate, team, or assumed business name unless the sponsoring broker has properly registered that name
choice_b: Sales agents are permitted to independently register and use any business name they choose without broker involvement
choice_c: TREC only regulates names used by brokers, not names used by sponsored sales agents
choice_d: There is no rule addressing agent-invented business names, so the conduct is fully compliant
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.154 requires that any alternate, team, or assumed business name used in advertising be properly registered, and a sponsored sales agent may not unilaterally adopt an unregistered name -- doing so bypasses both the broker's registration responsibility and the broker's oversight of advertising under that name.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.154 (Registration and Use of Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names Used in Advertisements)

question: A brokerage's compliance checklist for a new advertising campaign, built around 22 TAC Sections 535.154 and 535.155, should verify that:
choice_a: Any team or assumed business name used is properly registered, the broker's name meets the required size ratio and appears in a readily noticeable location, and any "sold" claim reflects actual involvement in that transaction
choice_b: The campaign has been pre-approved by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission before any local publication
choice_c: Only the sponsoring broker's personal cell phone number needs to appear anywhere in the ad, with no other content requirements
choice_d: Team names and assumed business names may be used interchangeably with no distinction in registration or scope
explanation: Texas real estate advertising compliance under 22 TAC Sections 535.154 and 535.155 turns on registered name use, the broker name size ratio, readily noticeable broker identification, and honest sold-credit claims -- there is no requirement for pre-clearance of ordinary local real estate advertising by the Federal Trade Commission, and team names/DBAs are not interchangeable.
source_note: 22 TAC Sections 535.154-535.155 (Advertisements; Alternate, Team and Assumed Business Names)

question: A broker structures a newly formed brokerage as an LLC in which the designated broker personally owns a 6 percent membership interest, with the remaining interest held by outside investors. Which combination of Section 1101.355 obligations applies to this entity?
choice_a: The designated broker must be an individual broker in active, good-standing status, and the entity must document errors and omissions insurance meeting the $1 million minimum occurrence limit because the designated broker's ownership is below 10 percent
choice_b: No special obligations apply because LLCs are categorically exempt from Section 1101.355
choice_c: Only the insurance requirement applies; the designated broker's good-standing status is irrelevant once the entity is formed
choice_d: The entity must convert to a sole proprietorship before it can hold a broker license
explanation: This scenario combines two distinct Section 1101.355 requirements that both apply here: the designated broker must be an individual broker in active status and good standing under subsection (b), and because that broker's ownership stake is under 10 percent, the entity must also document the required $1 million minimum errors and omissions insurance under subsection (a)(2).
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.355(a)(2), (b) (Additional General Eligibility Requirements for Business Entities)

question: A broker who has been licensed and physically operating from an office in Oklahoma, and has never maintained an office in Texas, applies for and receives a Texas broker license. Regarding the Texas fixed-office requirement, this broker:
choice_a: Qualifies as a nonresident broker under Section 1101.552(d) and is not required to maintain a place of business in Texas
choice_b: Is automatically denied a Texas license because Texas requires every broker to maintain an in-state office
choice_c: Must relocate permanently to Texas within 10 days of licensure
choice_d: Is treated identically to a resident broker with no distinction whatsoever
explanation: Section 1101.552(d) specifically exempts a nonresident licensed broker -- one whose business is based outside Texas -- from the fixed-office-in-Texas requirement that otherwise applies to resident brokers under subsection (a).
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.552(d) (Fixed Office Required; Change of Address)
